cards.front: Whose directions override a signal, and what must you do at a steady red light?
cards.back: Drivers obey every signal unless an officer directs otherwise, and officer orders stand even against ordinary law, with steady red demanding a stop ahead of the crosswalk or intersection before any lawful right turn or any left turn joining one one-way street from another, always yielding to pedestrians and legal intersection users.

cards.front: What do flashing red, steady and flashing yellow, and green signals and arrows each require?
cards.back: Flashing red means stop fully then go when safe while cross traffic may roll on, steady yellow orders a safe stop or a cautious clearing, flashing yellow orders slower caution, flashing yellow left arrows permit left turns against yielding to oncoming cars, steady green permits straight or turning travel with intersection watchfulness, green arrows beside red permit careful arrow-direction travel after yielding, and plain green lefts yield to all oncoming traffic.

cards.front: How does a steady red differ from a flashing red?
cards.back: Steady red stops before turns that stay conditional, while flashing red stops fully before a safe unconditioned go.

cards.front: How do steady yellow, flashing yellow, and a flashing yellow left arrow differ?
cards.back: Steady yellow demands a safe stop or cautious clearing, flashing yellow only slower caution, and flashing yellow left arrows add oncoming-yield duty.

cards.front: How does a steady green differ from a green arrow beside a red light?
cards.back: Steady green goes with intersection vigilance and yielding lefts, while green arrows beside red go carefully in the arrow's path after yielding.

cards.front: What four jobs do traffic signs do?
cards.back: Traffic signs warn of hidden hazards ahead, guide travelers along routes, publish local rules and habits, and regulate speed and movement.

cards.front: What does each sign color mean?
cards.back: Sign colors read red for stop, yield, or posted orders, green for allowed moves and direction, blue for motorist services, yellow for warning, black and white for regulation, orange for construction and maintenance, reflective orange for varied signs, and brown for recreation and scenery.

cards.front: What does each sign shape mean?
cards.back: Sign shapes read octagon for stop only, horizontal rectangle for guides, triangle for yield only, pennant for no-passing advance notice, diamond for hazard warnings, vertical rectangle for regulations, pentagon for school zones and crossings, and circle for railroad advance notice, with warning signs demanding attention, obedience, and posted-speed slowing under violation risk.

cards.front: Which colors and shapes go with stopping, yielding, warning, work zones, and recreation?
cards.back: Red orders, yellow warns, orange flags work zones, and brown guides recreation, matched by octagon stops, triangle yields, diamond warnings, and pennant no-pass notices.

decks.module: Warning signs for curves and roadway changes

cards.front: Which early warnings flag signals, low clearance, divided highways, added lanes, curves, side roads, and rough roads?
cards.back: Warning signs call for different responses. Check the posted height before entering an underpass; a median sign announces divided traffic; an added-lane sign means watch the new lane without merging. At a right-then-left curve, reduce speed, stay right and avoid passing. Watch for vehicles from a joining road, slow for rough pavement and heed warnings of a signal or crossing traffic ahead.
cards.memory_hook: Match each warning to its response

cards.front: Which warnings flag sharp turns, winding roads, divided-highway ends, wet roads, curves, crossroads, and lane reductions?
cards.back: Further warnings flag sharp arrowed turns, winding roads, divided-highway endings with returning two-way traffic, wet roads forbidding sudden moves, right-lane discipline against left-side oncoming cars, gradual arrowed curves, crossroads needing all-direction looks, and shrinking lane counts.

cards.front: How should you respond to warnings for reverse curves, sharp turns, winding roads, and gradual curves?
cards.back: For reverse curves, sharp turns and gradual curves, reduce speed, stay right and avoid passing. For a winding road, travel slowly and cautiously without passing.
cards.memory_hook: Slow for curves; heed each instruction

decks.module: Warning signs for junctions and surfaces

cards.front: Which warnings mark T and Y junctions, merges, pedestrians, schools, loose gravel, and obstructions?
cards.back: More warnings mark T and Y junctions, merging lanes, heavy pedestrian zones, schools needing sudden-stop readiness, loose gravel forbidding sharp braking or turns, edge and pier obstruction markers, and short-alignment change markers.

cards.front: Which warnings flag must-turns, dips, soft shoulders, narrow bridges, highway junctions, double turns, and icy bridges?
cards.back: Still more warnings order T must-turns with yielding, dip slowdowns, soft-shoulder caution, narrow-bridge care, highway-junction looks and stop readiness, double sharp turns, winter ice-bridge gentleness, and night-alignment delineators.

cards.front: How do junction warnings differ from surface warnings?
cards.back: Junction warnings cover T, Y, merges, and must-turns, while surface warnings cover gravel, dips, soft shoulders, and ice.

cards.front: Which warnings cover islands, bridge rails, entering trucks, narrow pavement, drop-offs, grooves, and disabled crossings?
cards.back: Continuing warnings allow either-side island passing, mark narrow-bridge rail ends, announce entering trucks, narrow pavements, pavement-to-earth transitions, edge drop-offs needing firm slow steering, grooved wet-weather grooves cautioning motorcyclists, and disabled or wheelchair crossings.

cards.front: Which warnings announce downgrades, metered ramps, humps, sharp curves, ending lanes, stop signs ahead, and animals?
cards.back: Final warnings announce downgrades possibly needing low gear, metered ramps with flashing yellows and red-green meters, sudden humps, sharp curves, ending right lanes merging left, stop signs ahead, and animals.

cards.front: What force do regulatory signs carry, and which lane and turn rules do they set?
cards.back: Regulatory signs bind like traffic laws, covering arrow-only turns, bus and carpool lanes weekday mornings six to nine, sight-limited yellow-line no-passing, double left-turn lanes with a mandatory left lane, disabled parking reserved to placarded vehicles, banned lefts, banned U-turns, and wrong-way one-way entry.

cards.front: What does a stop sign require, and what other speed and passing rules do regulatory signs set?
cards.back: More regulations order full stops with yielding and careful starts ahead of crosswalks and signs for every vehicle since slowing never suffices, plus advisory curve speeds, passing bans, slower-right discipline, safe ramp-exit speeds, posted day and night maximums, truck bans, and rightward island guidance.

cards.front: How does a stop sign differ from an advisory curve speed?
cards.back: Stop signs force full stops with yielding starts for every vehicle, while advisory speeds merely cap safe curve travel.

cards.front: Which regulatory signs cover one-way entry, merging, school speeds, red-light cameras, double white lines, and shoulders?
cards.back: Further regulations bar opposite-direction one-way entry, command merge-and-yield manners, enforce flashing-yellow school speeds with child watchfulness, warn of red-light cameras, forbid double-white-line crossings, protect green-arrow lefts while urging caution, reserve shoulders for breakdown and emergency stops, close roads to detours, and merge all traffic single-file.

cards.front: How do all-way stops, the far-left lane, center lanes, and right-turn lanes work?
cards.back: Still more regulations mark divided-highway crossovers, ban wireless devices in school zones, run all-way stops by arrival order with right-side ties, push slower traffic off the passing-only far-left lane, confine center lanes to slowing or stopping left turns, green-light left turns, force right-lane right turns, and post advisory turn speeds.

cards.front: How do all-way stop order, protected green arrows, and center turn lanes work together?
cards.back: All-way stops run by arrival with right-side ties, protected green arrows stop oncoming yet still want caution, and center lanes serve slowing lefts while far-left lanes serve passing.

cards.front: What do guide signs, railroad advance signs, crossbucks, and emergency notification signs tell you?
cards.back: Guide signs orient strangers, rail advance signs warn within a few hundred feet to slow, ready a stop, and never race trains, crossbucks stand at every crossing showing track counts with slow-look-listen yielding, and emergency notification signs carry railroad numbers plus national inventory numbers pinpointing crossings.

cards.front: What do route markers, mileposts, and lane-use control signals tell you?
cards.back: More guides point litter barrels a mile ahead and at rest areas, Texas and interstate markers name roads, overhead arrows assign route lanes, interstate mileposts pace emergencies every mile, exit-ahead lanes, short urban state highways, business branches, distance boards, and lane-use signals where red crosses close lanes, steady yellow crosses warn of lane-control changes, and green arrows open lanes.

cards.front: How do railroad advance signs, crossbucks, and lane-use red crosses and green arrows differ?
cards.back: Advance rail signs warn hundreds of feet out, crossbucks mark every crossing with track counts, red crosses close lanes, and green arrows open them.

cards.front: What must you do at lowering rail gates, and how do center lines and center turn lanes work?
cards.back: Gates demand stops at first flash before lowering and holds until raising with dark lights, rail stops land fifteen to fifty feet out on flaggers, red flashers with bells, or any train warnings, and markings show two-lane rural right-of-center discipline with broken-line passing only, free one-way lane choice with early turn positioning, center lanes entered solely to slow or stop for safe lefts, multi-lane double-yellow respect with slower-right habits, and center lanes never for passing or through travel.

cards.front: What do broken and solid lines permit, and how far from rails do you stop?
cards.back: Broken lines permit safe passing, solid yellow forbids it, and rail stops land fifteen to fifty feet from the rails.

cards.front: What do solid and broken yellow lines, crosswalks, stop lines, and solid or double white lines mean?
cards.back: Solid yellow lines on the driver's side ban passing while broken lines allow safe passes and lane changes, white crosswalks define walker zones with stops ahead of them when signs, signals, or walkers require, white stop lines demand stops behind them, solid white edges and channelizers discourage crossing, left-edge interstate yellow forbids leftward travel, and double solid white forbids all crossing.

cards.front: Where do crosswalks and stop lines place your stop, and how do single and double solid white differ?
cards.back: Crosswalks and stop lines fix where stops land, solid white discourages crossing, and double solid white bans it outright.

cards.front: What do crash barrels, hearing-impaired flags, and orange work-zone devices tell you, and what happens to fines there?
cards.back: Impact-cushion barrels lessen crash severity near solid obstacles or frequent-crash areas. Slow for a hearing-impaired flag on a bicycle; on a motor vehicle it alerts others. Orange is the basic work-zone-device color. Expect signs, barricades, panels, drums, cones, tubes, arrow panels and flaggers; prepare to reduce speed or stop, change lanes and react to workers or equipment. Most work signs are diamonds, with some rectangles. Traffic fines double for construction-zone violations when workers are present.

cards.front: What color marks work-zone devices, and when do fines double there?
cards.back: Work-zone traffic devices use orange as their basic color. A traffic violation in a construction zone carries double fines when workers are present.

cards.front: How should you respond to channelizers, barricade stripes, arrow panels, and flaggers?
cards.back: Channelizing devices with night lights order slowing, safe lane changes, late-merger wariness, reduced speed to the zone-end sign, and checked returns, barricade stripes point the passing side by downward slope, arrow panels day and night assign lanes past closures, orange-clad flaggers with paddles and flags command in-lane stops without veering and motionless waits, and remote auto-flaggers plus pilot cars, warnings, and temp signals may assist.

cards.front: Which way do barricade stripes point you, and what do flaggers expect?
cards.back: Stripe slopes point the passing side, and flaggers demand in-lane stops with motionless waits for their signal.

cards.front: What is the penalty for defying warning signs or barricades, and where do slow-moving emblems belong?
cards.back: Defying warning signs, markings, or barricades is a misdemeanor fining one to two hundred dollars, doubled in staffed work zones and rising to Class B up to two thousand dollars and one hundred eighty days in jail at flooded roads, while slow-moving emblems belong solely on machines capped at twenty-five miles per hour including animal-drawn rigs, never elsewhere or on fixed objects, except in-zone construction machines and towed implements trailing emblemed movers.

recap_hooks.text: Officers override signals, and a steady red means stop before the crosswalk.
Flashing red means stop, then go when safe; flashing yellow means slow down with caution.
Green arrows beside red allow careful travel in the arrow's direction after yielding.
Signs warn, guide, inform, and regulate.
Red stops, yellow warns, orange marks work zones, and brown guides recreation.
An octagon means stop, a triangle means yield, and a diamond warns.

recaps.module: Warning signs for curves and roadway changes

recap_hooks.text: Reverse curves, sharp turns and gradual curves require slowing, keeping right and no passing; winding roads require slow, careful driving without passing.

recaps.module: Warning signs for junctions and surfaces

recap_hooks.text: Junction warnings cover T and Y junctions, merges, and must-turns.
On loose gravel avoid sharp braking or turns; bridges may ice in winter.
On edge drop-offs steer firmly and slow down; downgrades may need a low gear.
Regulatory signs bind like traffic laws.
A stop sign means a full stop for every vehicle; slowing never suffices.
At all-way stops, go in arrival order, and the driver on the right wins ties.
Never cross a double white line.
Crossbucks mark every railroad crossing; slow, look, and listen.
Over lanes, a red cross closes the lane and a green arrow opens it.
Stop at the first flash of crossing gates and wait until they rise and the lights go dark.
Broken lines allow safe passing; solid yellow on your side forbids it.
Stop behind white stop lines, and never cross double solid white.
Orange devices mark work zones, and fines double where workers are present.
Follow flaggers and stop in your lane when told.
Defying warning signs or barricades brings fines, with Class B penalties at flooded roads.
